speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: UNITED STATES
subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF VESSELS INTO ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) asked about recent press reports concerning the activities of United States naval vessels in the Canadian Arctic during the coming summer. I am not sure exactly what report he was referring to, though I understand there was one in the April 3 issue of the Montreal Gazette and another in the edition of the Financial Post dated April 6.

subtopic: UNITED STATES
subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF VESSELS INTO ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext: No, it was one which appeared in the Christian Science Monitor.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: UNITED STATES
subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF VESSELS INTO ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext: Well, I have not seen the one in the Christian Science Monitor, but I assume it would be along the same lines.

subtopic: UNITED STATES
subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF VESSELS INTO ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext: Yes, it was much the same as the one which appeared in the Gazette.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: UNITED STATES
subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF VESSELS INTO ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext:
These stories were apparently based on a recent United States navy press release. When arrangements were being made for the construction of the distant early warning line Canada and the United States agreed that the United States should be responsible for the sea supply of the D.E.W. line while it was being built.
It was realized that because of the amount of material involved and the urgency of the operation, a large number of special vessels
would be required which Canada was not in a position to supply. At the time this agreement was reached, however, the United States was informed that once the line was in operation Canada might wish to assume responsibility for the annual resupply. Arrangements have already been completed for the Northern Transportation Company to resupply the western portion of the D.E.W. line beginning in the summer of 1958. Discussions are under way to determine if the Department of Transport can assume the responsibility for supplying the eastern portion of the line in connection with their other responsibilities in the Arctic.
As a result of the agreement I just mentioned the United States navy has been sending two convoys into the Canadian Arctic for the past two summers. One of these has emanated from Seattle and the other from New York or Boston. These convoys have had the task of supplying all the United States installations in the north, including those in Alaska and Greenland as well as in Canada. This may be one reason why the number of ships involved seems to be large. Actually only a portion of each convoy enters Canadian waters. The operation this summer will be similar in both size and organization to that of the past two summers.
As in other years Canada will be well represented on both convoys. During the past two summers there have been both official government representatives as well as technical observers working with the commander of each task force. H.M.C.S. Labrador has provided icebreaker support for the eastern task force and the Royal Canadian Air Force has carried out a series of ice reconnaissances. Similar arrangements will be in effect again this summer.
Canada has always been consulted when the plans for the convoys were being made each year. This year, for instance, representatives of the Royal Canadian Navy and the Royal Canadian Air Force attended a series of meetings held in Seattle on February 5 to make arrangements for the sea supply of the western Arctic, and a senior Canadian naval officer attended a meeting in Washington on March 25 when the details of the eastern Arctic convoy were being worked out. Incidentally, each year the United States navy has been required to apply for a waiver of the
3186	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry provisions of the Canada Shipping Act, since the cargo ships they charter operate in Canadian coastal waters.
The suggestion that this summer's task force is being organized to discover a northwest passage rather than supply the D.E.W. line and other United States installations is, I am afraid, the fruit of a rather active imagination. During the past two summers a great deal of hydrographic work has been done jointly by Canadian and United States agencies in connection with the sea supply of the D.E.W. line, and except for the area around Boothia peninsula the task is now almost complete. Plans have been made to finish the work during the coming summer by having both Canadian and United States vessels work at the problem from opposite sides. H.M.C.S. Labrador will proceed from the Atlantic to the vicinity of Prince Regent inlet and carry out survey work there, while the United States navy icebreaker Storis and two other United States coastguard survey ships will carry out similar work on the western side of Boothia peninsula. H.M.C.S. Labrador will be surveying Bellot strait which provides a channel between the eastern and western Arctic, and if it is found that water and ice conditions are suitable the three United States navy vessels may attempt to pass through Bellot strait and accompany the Labrador south to the Atlantic.
Useful hydrographic information will undoubtedly be collected during this joint project by the United States and Canadian navies, and it will be interesting to see if larger ships can pass through Bellot strait. We already know that small ships can navigate the strait because the Royal Canadian Mounted Police vessel St. Roch completed the passage in 1942.
If larger vessels can navigate this route it will provide a useful alternative for ships carrying supplies to the area, but it will probably always remain a second choice since ice conditions in the vicinity are known to be difficult in most years. Any ship wishing to pass from the Atlantic to the Pacific or vice versa would probably follow the route farther north through Lancaster and Viscount Melville sounds, which H.M.C.S. Labrador used in 1955.

subtopic: UNITED STATES
subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF VESSELS INTO ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister whether the Canadian government considers these waters to be Canadian territorial waters, and, if so, whether the United States government admits that such is the case?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: UNITED STATES
subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF VESSELS INTO ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext:
I do not know whether we can interpret the fact that they did comply with our requirement that they obtain a waiver of the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act as an admission


that these are territorial waters, but if they were not territorial waters there would be no point in asking for a waiver under the Canada Shipping Act.

subtopic: UNITED STATES
subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF VESSELS INTO ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext: There is no doubt, then, that the Canadian government at least considers them as territorial waters?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: UNITED STATES
subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF VESSELS INTO ARCTIC WATERS
speechtext: Oh, yes, the Canadian government considers that these are Canadian territorial waters, and we make it a condition of the consent we have given to these arrangements that they apply for a waiver from the provisions that would otherwise apply in Canadian territorial waters.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPLY OF PREMIER OF BRITISH COLUMBIA TO FEDERAL OFFER
speechtext: I wish to address a question to the Prime Minister. Has the Prime Minister received any official response from the premier of British Columbia with respect to the government's offer to co-operate with that government in the matter of public power development on the Columbia?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPLY OF PREMIER OF BRITISH COLUMBIA TO FEDERAL OFFER
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, to my knowledge there has not been any communication since the possibility was expressed of the government being interested in the development of power on the Columbia after negotiations with the United States government have been completed.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPLY OF PREMIER OF BRITISH COLUMBIA TO FEDERAL OFFER
speechtext: May I ask why it is necessary to wait until the negotiations are completed before any attempt is made to reach agreement with the province of British Columbia?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPLY OF PREMIER OF BRITISH COLUMBIA TO FEDERAL OFFER
speechtext:
I do not
know that it is necessary, but those negotiations aim at retaining for Canada as much as possible of all the benefits, either upstream or downstream, which might result from regulating the flow of the Columbia river. I think they would very probably affect the kind of physical works that would be erected for the purpose of making that control of the flow as effective as possible.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPLY OF PREMIER OF BRITISH COLUMBIA TO FEDERAL OFFER
speechtext: Does that not mean that it may be many months or even years before anything can be done about the Columbia river? Our understanding was that they could proceed very shortly to build the Mica dam.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPLY OF PREMIER OF BRITISH COLUMBIA TO FEDERAL OFFER
speechtext: Of course, I would imagine that if the government of British Columbia wished to proceed with the building of the Mica dam they would communicate with us, have the plans prepared and have them dealt with as expeditiously as they might find it in their interest to do so in conformity with the provisions of the legislation that is applicable. It may very well be that it will be considered by the government of British Columbia that the dam should be a provincial work and not a work erected by the federal government.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPLY OF PREMIER OF BRITISH COLUMBIA TO FEDERAL OFFER
speechtext:
Does that statement mean that there need not necessarily be delay until negotiations with the United States are completed, and that this co-operative arrangement could be started at once?
[Mr. Knowles.)

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPLY OF PREMIER OF BRITISH COLUMBIA TO FEDERAL OFFER
speechtext: It means that we will give consideration to any proposal the British Columbia government may feel it should make at any time.

speechtext: 335. Transportation-movement of mail by land, air and water, including administration, and to authorize and provide for the adjustment, as of October 1, 1956, of rural mail delivery contracts in effect on that date or entered into by way of renewal after that date, under the provisions of subsection (2) of section 33 of the Post Office Act, notwithstanding paragraphs (b) and (c) thereof, $51,940,991.

Mr. Chairman, I have only a few words I would like to say at this time concerning this item, and they have to do with the mail carrier service in the rural areas in the interior of British Columbia. In view of the fact that there was a substantial surplus in the Post Office Department last year I feel there should be a review of the situation that arises in many rural post offices where mail has to be carried from the post office to the railway trains or other distributing points.
I mentioned this to the minister a year or so ago when he was first given the portfolio, and I think he is quite aware of the necessity for doing something to alleviate the situation that exists in some of these rural areas. I do not think it is reasonable that the post office department should show a large surplus every year. A little experimentation along the lines of giving slightly improved service in these rural areas would be well worth while even if the Post Office Department showed a deficit for a year.
The most recent case I have in mind is one which I think is under investigation by

the Post Office Department at this time. I am referring to the situation that obtains at Dunster, in my own riding, and there are others which arise from time to time.
I would hope the Post Office Department would consider doing a little more in the way of increasing the remuneration paid to the people who carry mail, particularly taking into consideration the prevailing wage scale in the area where the work is performed. This is a factor which I fully realize is difficult to overcome in many instances where you have a high wage scale prevailing in one part of the country and a low wage scale prevailing in another. Under these circumstances it is difficult to have a uniform policy that is going to apply across Canada. However, I think a closer look should be given to the matter to see if the service can be improved somewhat at the rural points.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate my hon. friend's remarks, and I have had conversations with him previously about the particular situation he has mentioned. We are trying to expand these services. We realize that in these distant areas where travelling may be difficult people are just as anxious to receive their mail as elsewhere, and we plan to expand these services further.
As regards the wages paid to the couriers, I might say that these services are performed under contract, as my hon. friend realizes, so the price paid the courier is the price at which he has tendered. However, in estimating what we consider to be a fair price for a contract we take into consideration the differential in wages in various parts of the country basing our calculations on the figures provided to us periodically by the Department of Labour.

Mr. Chairman, I would like once again to draw to the attention of the authorities the question of new post office facilities at Saskatoon. I use the word "authorities" because the Postmaster General will hasten to assure me it is now the business of the Minister of Public Works. Plans for new post office facilities at Saskatoon have already been authorized. I suppose "authorized" is to be preferred to the word "okayed" which was on the tip of my tongue; it is amazing how slang creeps into our language. Anyway, "okayed" is what I mean.
I have a press dispatch which appeared in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of April 2, which reached me only today. The headline reads, "Postal Business Tops $1,000,000 for First Time", and this of course refers to the city of

I have two matters to draw to the attention of the Postmaster General, one of which is that the post office in Saskatoon is now responsible for the mail delivery, at some distance from the centre of the city, to the residents of the town of Sutherland, which was amalgamated last year with the city of Saskatoon. The mail is now delivered from the central office in Saskatoon rather than from the little local post office at Sutherland where the people used to call for their mail. May I say that is a great advantage to the people of Sutherland. They appreciate the action of the post office in this regard, and though I might point out that we thought it was a trifle slow in coming nevertheless the conditions were fulfilled.
However, the point is that the central office has the extra business to handle. If one were to read the statement from the postmaster at Saskatoon to which I have referred one would see that business in every sphere has increased. I am merely seeking to point out that with the growth of our city the need for the new post office facilities is becoming greater and greater. We already have the assurance of the Postmaster General that new facilities will be provided any time as far as he is concerned.
Another matter with which I wish to deal concerns the extra delivery men for Sutherland. There was another statement made by the Saskatoon postmaster which I quoted a month or two ago when I spoke on this question. The local postmaster stated that he did not want to undergo another Christmas rush like the one last year unless he had these added facilities.
One must know that if it involves a new building, these facilities cannot be provided before the next Christmas rush, but they could be provided and ready for the one which would come after that. Owing to the great increase in population-the population is now some 72,000 and is going up-it seems

to me that these facilities should be provided and the post office officials and workers should not be asked to handle that immense amount of business with the facilities with which they are now provided.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister could make some further statement as to what progress is being made as the result of recommendations to the department with regard to a general increase in the remuneration to rural mail couriers. They perform a vitally important service, and quite often put up with conditions which do not exist as far as many public servants are concerned. speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I did announce some time ago in the house that on my instructions a survey had been made last fall and that every case was being looked into. This is being done at the present time; the adjustments have been determined, and these rural mail couriers will be advised before the end of this month of the adjustment that has been made in their contracts.
Thank you very much. In that connection I take it that each case is being judged on its merits and that there is no formula.

Each case has been looked into individually. This procedure has to be followed because in some cases the courier had made an application within a month or two before the decision was made. As he could make this application under the law if he could meet the terms of the section of the act, the application had been processed and he had already received that increase. Naturally, therefore, in those circumstances his case had been settled and he would not receive as much as the others whose cases had not been considered for some years. That made it necessary for each case to be looked into individually.

Could the minister give some indication as to what percentage of the contracts are being increased; just a rough idea?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs

May I ask the minister whether this is a change in policy on the part of the department?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
It is a change in policy in this manner, Mr. Chairman. Under the postal act, increases in contracts for rural mail delivery can be dealt with under certain circumstances, one of them being that the contract has to have been in effect for two years, and there must have been a lapse of at least two years before an application can be considered for a new increase in the price of a contract.
The situation which arose was that in a case where, for instance, the contractor had received an increase in his contract say four years ago, after his contract had been running two years. He had made an application which had been examined, and his contract had been increased. When the contract was renewed this constituted a new contract, and he could not ask for a further increase until two years had run on the new contract, so he was still operating on the price determined four years previously and the act, as it exists now, would not permit him to make an application or permit the department to give him an increase on that contract.
By providing an estimate as we have done this year it does, however, give the department the authority to look into every one of these contracts and, regardless of the length of time the contract has been in effect or the time which has elapsed since the last increase, to make an adjustment if it is deemed necessary.

May I ask a question of the minister; perhaps this occurs when the old contract is up, say, and new contracts are called for. Supposing the successful contractor's tender is lower than what is paid to the old contractor. Is there a readjustment made after that, or just what is the situation?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: If it was before October 1, yes.
Of last year?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The item in the estimates mentions October 1, and if it was before October 1, 1956, there would be a readjustment; there have been quite a few cases like that.
But supposing it was not before October 1, what is the result? Say it was up next year?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: He would have to wait two years under the act.

The policy in the past seemed to have been a very fair one; what is bothering me now is the answer given by the minister to the hon. member for Royal a few minutes ago.
In the past, if I have understood the policy correctly, you have tried to use the rural mail couriers and treat them alike in so far as mileage and so on were concerned. I say this because I have letters on file over the last two years in which they point out that a certain man may have asked for an increase. Another man say 20 miles, 30 miles or 40 miles away under similar conditions was only getting so much, therefore this was fair for this particular rural mail courier.
Now, as I understand it, the policy of the department is that they will pay a rural mail courier on the standard of wages he might earn if he were working in that community in some other industry. I do not think that is quite the same as treating them on the grounds on which they have been treated in the past, because a man could very well earn $2,500 a year in one community and 50 miles away he could not earn that amount of money. Therefore if you are going to base it on the Department of Labour figures I think you are going to have an irregular level of contract prices, and in that case it will not be as satisfactory as it has been in the past.
I must say that in the last few years it seems to me the department has been using very good judgment in increasing these rates for rural mail couriers. That is a fair way of handling it. As I pointed out a year ago, certain other practices which are creeping into this department are not to my liking. This is another thing of the same kind.
I suppose it is early to talk about it; we shall have to wait for a year and see, but I am afraid I shall find that some mail carriers in my constituency will receive the increase while others, using the same equipment, travelling the same distances and working the same hours, will not receive it. I want to see all rural mail carriers treated in the same way, and I think their remuneration should be based on the mileage and service given, as was done in the past, if I understand the position correctly, and not on local wages or employment conditions.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member that his fears are not justified. We are applying the same principle in this connection, but we are being more generous in view of the increased cost of operation and the increase in wages generally. This policy was followed because it was so specified in the act, and the section of the act referring to this increase said the increased amounts were not to exceed the amounts paid generally for comparable services in the same area.
This is the policy we have followed in making these readjustments, and we take into consideration the hourly wage for similar work in the area, the distance to be covered and the number of boxes to be served. Of course the distance covered and the number of boxes would bring in the time element; the greater the distance covered and the more boxes, the longer it will take for the route to be completed. That, together with the hourly wage, will give us an idea as to what the general average adjustment should be, and that is the principle we have followed all along. I can assure the hon. member that what he fears will not take place. I am quite certain of that.

May I ask this further question. I recall that in former times these contracts were usually renewed by tender. Tenders were called for when a contract was to be given out. Is there not a tendency nowadays not to call for tenders but simply to renew the existing contract?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No, there has been no change in that respect. This is being done purely to adjust the prices of contracts now in effect. It makes no change in the rest of the policy.

As the minister knows, I have a little empire right in the centre of the province of Ontario. Generally speaking routes are comparable, though there be one or two exceptions. I think the combination of mileage and boxes is a fair way of estimating the cost of distribution or the price that should be paid.
A year or more ago I do not know exactly what happened, but one contractor lost his contract to another who had probably underbid him by a few cents. Since that time, it is true, a few contractors have applied for and obtained small increases, but most of the couriers in my area are veterans or people rising in years or incapacitated in one way or another, and they are very nervous about applying for increases. Even though they feel their remuneration should be increased, they are very hesitant about making application in case they should lose their jobs. I understand that all the contracts will now be examined and put on a fair and equitable basis.

I am informed that as T.C.A. continues to develop this service the mail carrying capacity will be increased.

Actually it is not a question of the capacity of the existing aircraft. New aircraft are coming into operation which will help deal with this situation within two or three years, but I am glad to learn that at the present time this seems to be under control.

will not pursue that matter.

The department has been doing some experimenting with the operation of its own trucking systems within metropolitan areas rather than letting contracts, as was done previously. What has been the experience of the department in that connection? Can we be given comparative cost figures for centres such as Windsor and Ottawa, where I believe the system has been in operation for some little time?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I am informed that it is only in Windsor that the department has been experimenting with the use of its own trucks. Parcel post delivery was being done in Ottawa by our own trucks and that was given up. As far as Windsor is concerned, we are still experimenting because the conditions under which we operate are changing and it is difficult for us to give a definite answer with respect to whether it would be to the advantage of the department. Such factors as the maintenance of trucks, salaries, accommodation in which to put the trucks, garage services and so on, vary from place to place. That has happened in Windsor, and it is very difficult for us to arrive at a definite answer.
Personally I have not yet been convinced that it would be an economical method of operation, and I do not envisage the Post Office Department operating a truck service and becoming a transport company throughout Canada, because my limited experience of trucking indicates that it is a very complex business and has to be operated with great efficiency in order to be profitable.

Since certain experimentation has been carried on in Windsor I think it would be interesting for the committee to have figures covering what the cost was under the contract system in the last year in which service was provided in that way and the cost in the first year in which the department operated its own trucks.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs

speechtext: As to those that are under the control of the department the figure is the same as it was last year, namely 500. We have not ordered more or installed more because we wanted a long enough period of time in which to judge the efficiency of these machines. They were installed over the last two years, I believe. We therefore waited for a period of time before ordering any new machines of that type in order to make sure they would be properly working machines. Can
the minister give us something a little more definite than that weasel word "eventually"?

should like to take just a moment on that point. I do not believe there is anything which brings greater convenience to a large section of the Canadian public than the installation of these stamp vending machines. Many people are not always in a position to be in possession of the postage stamps

they need. Many people also must mail urgent letters after post offices are closed, as well as other places where stamps are sold. The department now has a machine which seems to be satisfactory. It is the sort of thing the minister could very well overlook unless his attention is drawn to it and he is urged to do it. I believe this is the last item, Mr. Chairman. I have had some correspondence with the Postmaster General for several years in connection with the people of Creighton, Saskatchewan, who are obliged to go over to the neighbouring province of Manitoba in order to buy their postage stamps. I might mention that this is the largest village in Canada. I wonder whether the Postmaster General could say anything about the possibility of these people buying their postage stamps in their own province. Since we started discussing this matter with the minister the population has gone up by about 300 per cent. That is in the last three or four years.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend is referring to the establishment of a post office. He would be out of order in speaking about that matter on this item, and I think he knows it. Will the Postmaster General comment on any changes which have occurred in the operation of the post office savings bank in the past year, whether its operations are extending or contracting and, most particularly, whether the department is continuing to

carry on the rather senseless practice, in my estimation at least, of operating post office savings banks in localities which are adequately served by private banks and where the operation of the post office savings bank is largely a matter of competing with the private commercial banks.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: There have been no changes as regards policy except that the rate of interest on deposits was raised from 2 per cent to 2J per cent in November, 1956. As regards the use of this savings bank service provided by the post office, I think I expressed my views fairly clearly last year on the matter. I believe it is a good service. I believe it serves a certain class of the population. I think it is something to be encouraged. My own personal views are that this service should be continued.

I should like to go on record as opposing the proposal made by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace. I might point out that this service is superior to the service that is being offered by the chartered banks. Any person in Canada who has the good fortune to have an account with the post office savings bank can get money at any place in Canada without paying exchange and without requiring any identification. I think most Canadians would object strenuously if the use of the post office savings banks should be limited only to places where there are no chartered banks. I see no reason why those who have post office saving bank accounts should not have the same facilities in a city like Ottawa or a city like Montreal as are available in these small communities where there are no chartered banks. I hope the minister will never yield to the suggestion that the post office savings banks be closed in all places except those that are too small to warrant a bank.

I can
appreciate the socialist viewpoint which has been expressed by the hon. member who has taken his seat and which seems to be concurred in by the government in its existing policy, as in so many other things.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: We are not ashamed of it, either.

No;
that is one of the regrettable things. The government has reached a point where it is not ashamed of being socialist in mind.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Branding a policy by name has never been an argument against it.
Unfortunately, because of the limitations on the debate, we cannot enter into a discussion about many of the particular socialist problems.
Would the Tories close these post office savings banks if they were to form a government?

I was
just coming to that. My remarks were made in the light of a report the post office issued about three years ago, which drew attention to the fact that the operation of this bank was costing the taxpayers close to $400,000, about $377,000 each year. The minister took issue with that last year, I must say in fairness to him, but we must also remember that these were highly qualified management consultants who made this report. They made the unequivocal statement that it was costing the taxpayers $377,000 a year.
The point I made before referred specifically to the operation of the post office savings bank in competition with the private banking system of the country. There was a point, Mr. Chairman, at which the post office savings bank might have been open a little longer and thus offer some additional facilities to the taxpayers. But even that has now gone by the board, since the majority of the private banks in residential areas are open in the evenings for the convenience of their customers. It would seem to me that the continued operation of these banks, which originally served a very definite purpose when our banking system in this country was not as extensive as it is today, is an unnecessary form of competition and an unnecessary duplication of service. In most cases it serves little useful purpose, but does cost the taxpayers a substantial amount of money.
The hon. member did not answer my question. Will the Tories abolish the post office savings bank if they ever form a government?
Wait until election time to fight the campaign. If you want to get into an election fight come into my riding; I should like to take one of you over the boards.

I am
not in a position to enunciate policy, which should properly come from the party leader and which will come in due course. But as a private individual I may say I am completely opposed to the intrusion of government on a competitive basis into operations which can be very effectively carried on by private business.

I should like to inform the house that I must correct two figures that were given in the statement I made yesterday at the resolution stage. Mr. Speaker, it is always somewhat difficult to follow the resolution stage of a bill just 24 hours later with second reading and expect that much can be said without some repetition. I shall do my best today, sir, not to

repeat anything I have said, but perhaps I may enlarge upon some of the comments I made yesterday.
First of all let me say that as this bill comes before the house it has its greatest impact, I think, in bringing home to us each year the tremendous sums which are required to carry out the operations of the railway company. I believe we are impressed each year as well by the fact that since the Canadian National Railway company is a crown corporation and subject to the whims, fancies and requirements of geography, politicians and considerations of that kind, it probably works under a much greater handicap in the transportation field than does its private competitor.
I think as well we must note each year that the railway company does have a more difficult job from the financing standpoint. It must come before the house each year and lay everything before it, because by the terms of reference under which it operates if there is any surplus at all in a year it is returned to the people in the form of dividends on the equity stock which the government holds, whereas the private railway company is in a position to add a little more readily to its reserves in addition to the usual amount of depreciation which can be obtained each year.
I am speaking from memory, sir, but my recollection is that the Canadian Pacific Railway as the result of last year's operation was able to retain several million dollars-I think as much as $20 million-from accrued earnings and transfer it to its reserves. This is something that is not available to the Canadian National Railways, even if that much money turned up as profit each year.
The requirement for large amounts of money for the operations of the Canadian National Railways will continue, and certainly it will continue on an ever-increasing scale in connection with the railway's financing of Trans-Canada Air Lines operations, because of course that company is just approaching a stage where large financial outlays will be required to cover the changeover from the piston engine phase of operation through the phase of the jet-propeller type of operation to straight jet operation. Tremendous amounts of money will be required for that purpose.
This is of special interest to us, because we must remember that this is money which the government of Canada ordinarily borrows in the bond market and on which it pays something like 3J per cent or 4 per cent interest. In relation to the bonds which the Canadian National holds, obviously those are fixed and in connection with the railway's financial

statement the amount is paid back to the company. However, in connection with the equity stock it holds, I think we will find that while this year has been exceptionally better than previous years, still the return on the government's money is something like li per cent or 2 per cent. Therefore even with fairly good years of operation we find it is necessary to fall slightly behind in the return which is received from the equity interest of the government as against the amount which must be paid when we go into the market to borrow funds to pay out for this preferred stock or lend to the company on this preferred stock issue.
I sincerely hope, sir, that with the growing importance of the northern areas of the country which the Canadian National Railway has always serviced we will keep in mind what the president of the railway said, to the effect that though it had been a great disadvantage to its competitive position with the Canadian Pacific Railway over the years the indications now are that with the increased development there and the increase in the gross national product it could represent a phase in the operation of the Canadian National Railways comparing in importance with the original opening up of the country which was performed by the Canadian Pacific Railway many years ago. If that should be a correct prediction then I think we can foresee a time when the Canadian National Railways will be returning to the government a fair equity return on its investment.
I mentioned one thing yesterday to which I think I might return today. That is that it is most difficult for us to understand why it is necessary for the Canadian National Railways to continue to be the financing agent for the national air line operations. That has been impressed upon me more and more each time I have been a member of the special committee on railways and shipping, and I recently asked the president of Canadian National Railways about this matter. On page 182 of the minutes of the committee he said-I am not going to read all the questions and answers-the following:
The history of it, of course, was in the days the Trans-Canada Air Lines was formed, and the Canadian National Railways provided a nucleus of an organization-provided a staff, in other words-to get the organization going. We still have a number of interlocking arrangements with them. For instance, we provide their legal services, we provide their medical services, we look after the treasury work, in the sense of the handling of their bank accounts, and things of that kind. But, over the years it is gradually drawing apart, and they are becoming more and more a completely independent organization in that respect. The reason we continue such operations as we do is, that we believe, between ourselves, that it is more economical to do so. We also provide a general secretary between the two companies as well.
82715-202J
Canadian National Railways
There was also a certain amount of discussion dealing with the question of whether it was easier and cheaper to finance the operation of the government's air line by making its requirements a part of the larger bloc financing required by the national railway. I think, as a matter of fact, you will find that this year's requirements of the railway are up about $50 million, and that approximately $20 million of the increase is required for the air line itself.
Now the air line is on a profitable basis, and has been for some period of time. As a matter of fact it is interesting for us to note that the net income this year, after provision for depreciation and all other fixed charges, was $1,556,212. It is most difficult for us to compare the operation of the air line with the Canadian Pacific Air Lines operation. The only comparison or standard we could go by is to take perhaps the air passenger miles flown. I see there are approximately four times the passenger miles flown by the government air line as compared with the Canadian Pacific Air Lines. The Canadian Pacific report indicates that there was a net profit on their air line operations of $525,000. I think, therefore, we can see an indication here that the government air line is maintaining a standard of profit which compares with the private operation.
Someone may say it is no more difficult for the government air line to carry out operations in far-flung areas of the country, perhaps where the return per passenger mile is not as great as that in a concentrated population. The government air line furthermore must carry out some of these operations in fulfilling its role in the public interest, but I may add that Canadian Pacific Air Line is also a pioneer in a great many respects with regard to thousands of miles of its operations and must, I think, be facing the same type of lower return on certain segments of its line. The over-all picture, however, would indicate some satisfaction to us in seeing these profits more or less on a comparable basis if we check the air passenger miles flown by each company.
Of course this government-operated air line is going to grow and grow. It seems evident that its financial requirements, first of all, can be handled on its own. There does not seem to be any reason now why there should be a continuation of our mixing its financial requirements with the national railway system, and I am quite sure that Trans-Canada Air Lines is in a position to stand on its own feet in that regard.
There was one other thing about which I have been thinking and which I mentioned very briefly the other day. I think there is

Canadian National Railways considerable reluctance when anybody says, "Well, why not sell the national air line?" There is a great deal of national pride in it; but I do not think, Mr. Speaker, we should simply continue and increase the number of crown corporations simply as an indication of the stature or the glory that must be attached to any single cabinet minister. Furthermore, I do not see a situation where the national air line, in some package deal, will be disposed of to some private interest. I mentioned the other day, however, that there was certainly a precedent set in Alberta where a gas collection and distribution company was being organized and the people were given the opportunity to buy into what was, I think, a crown corporation.
The financial structure of this air line at the moment is not so great that it would frighten any people involved in the floating of bond issues or equity stock issues in any way at all. As a matter of fact its requirements, as I see the right-hand side of this financial statement, are much less than many of the current operations of large companies in Canada today. I mentioned these figures yesterday in general; I did not have the statement before me, but the company has notes payable to Canadian National Railways of $20 million and debenture at 3| per cent, maturing January 1,	1973,
for $20 million. It also has reserves of $6 million for insurance, and for overhaul $393,939. The total capital stock including 250,000 shares of common stock at a par value of $100 per share amounts to $5 million. Its surplus as of January 1 was $6,267,000.
I specifically mention these figures because, of course, they are the amounts, plus an amount for good will, which would have to be replaced if there was any indication of seeing that this stock was generally held by the public and not by the government through its agent the Canadian National Railways. I do not know what is involved here, but subject to what might be considered as an item for good will probably the overall picture of about $60 million would cover the lower right-hand corner, as accountants say, of the balance sheet of the company.
As a matter of fact, if there were debentures issued for $50 million or $60 million almost the same type of unit transaction could be used in seeing that the ownership of this company was spread throughout the public generally, as is the method used in many types of financing operations. If there were $100 debentures units, there would be $50,000,000 involved in 500,000 units, and using a par value of $10 for the common stock I think we could set it up on the basis

of unit debentures, each unit at $100 entitling a person to buy five common shares at $10 each.
Someone will say that once you do a thing like that, of course, you are leaving it open to the purchase of large blocks of shares by foreign investors. Well, Mr. Speaker, in this case I do not think that would be possible, because the Aeronautics Act provides that no more than 40 per cent of the controlling interest in such a company can be owned by persons other than Canadian citizens.

But when he was making the offer last year apparently he restricted it to one company and attached about $150 million worth of assistance to them. In those circumstances, why would not anyone say it would be much better for the people of Canada to build the pipe line?
I have just mentioned one of the considerations which I think might arise and one of the difficulties which I think would be involved in connection with the type of operation of which the minister has been speaking. There is a restriction under our act which deals with aeronautics and foreign control cannot occur in this field, but we can see what happened in the Alberta instance. According to newspaper reports many people in the street were interested in investing in an enterprise concerned with the collection and distribution of gas out there, and I am convinced that the same thing would happen here; the people of Canada would become financially interested, and we would not continue to have the remote type of control we have in this case.
Let's face it. I do not think the system of government in this country or in any similar parliamentary democracy was designed to supervise the continued expansion of crown-owned corporations. I do not think that is our function here. I do not believe it is our function to be spending as much time as we are spending in reviewing the operations of these companies. Ordinarily the shareholders of companies can ensure that those companies

are operating efficiently, and I think to a great extent it has become a waste of time to put hon. members through this mill year after year.
Here is an opportunity to see whether we cannot stop this type of management, reverse this trend in government affairs and return to a more business like way of handling operations of this kind. I shall say no more on this particular subject, though there are a few more things I should like to say about the railway situation.
I said earlier that the extension of rail lines, though it will bring undoubted advantages, particularly in the north land, involves also the danger that the profits or returns, if any, from such expansion will not compensate for the capital expenditure necessary for such extensions.
Prospects of a sound financial position could all be lost if we were to go through a period, as once we did in this country, when pressure groups all over the place were demanding that lines be built whether or not they were likely to prove an economic operation. I think a good criterion to use would be this; that if there are any particular areas in this country with regard to which it is argued a railway line would certainly be a sound proposition, then perhaps-and I suggested this last year-the time has come when we should say to the people in these particular areas, "Are you prepared to put your guarantee on the debentures which must be issued in order to carry out this type of expansion?" As a matter of fact it will be difficult for us to put such a proposal because, if I understand the accounting system of the railway company correctly, it is almost impossible to determine which of the operations are profitable and which are not.
There is another thing I might mention. There was an indication in connection with the figures concerning the over-all railway operation that the company is facing a depreciation problem, and there was also an indication that the railway might have to come back to parliament for legislation enabling it to deal with that problem.
The matter arose in this way. . The railway has a dieselization program under way, and naturally the ordinary type of depreciation is taking place with regard to the new locomotives.	But back in 1940 a new
depreciation plan was set up for the remainder of the steam locomotives. I think they were given a residual life of about 30 years from 1930. But there is an indication in the auditor's report that under this depreciation plan, at the end of five or six years there will be a sum of $30 million in steam locomotive equipment which will
Canadian National Railways not have been written off; and there was an indication from the auditor that it would perhaps have been wiser if provision for this residual depreciation had been started this year.
If it had started, then based on a period of five or six years another $6 million would have to be taken off the profit figures of the railway this year, thus reducing the figure which was presented to the committee and to the house. I do not know whether this depreciation item is being taken into account next year, and I think the parliamentary assistant might indicate what plans the government have made, if any, to take care of this situation. If they do nothing, then at the end of five years we shall find that for several years the railway has shown an illusory profit figure. Someone is going to draw a line, put $30 million under it, and we will find ourselves $30 million in the hole. I think the government should tell us what it intends to do about this.
Before closing, I should like to repeat that the railway is in the black. It is in the black even though its present operations cannot be compared with the ordinary types of operation of a private company in other fields or, even with its competitor in this particular field. I think for their service and loyalty the officers and employees of the company deserve a great deal of commendation.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to add a very few observations to those made before we rose for lunch. It is merely stating the obvious to say that Canadian National Railways has now become an institution of vast importance in our lives. The figures with which they deal have now grown so that they are far larger than those of many government departments, and they show every sign of increasing.
It is a fortunate thing that we have in the president of the road a man of wide experience and a man who has regard to the impact of his organization on the country's whole economy. I quote his own words with regard to the capital program, as found at page 209 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the sessional committee:
We have just slowed the whole thing down on the basis that we are attempting to do too much and that the country is attempting to do too much having regard to its productive capacity.
I quote that merely to show that I feel we have at the head of the railway organization a man whose wide grasp of affairs enables him to see the economy as a whole. It is almost ironical to look back to the twenties, when a leading newspaper in Canada published certain articles under the title, "The Whisper of Death", which were designed really to cast doubt on the possibility of operating this conglomeration of roads which had been brought together under the name of Canadian National Railways. As we look back across the intervening decades we take comfort and satisfaction from the fact that the difficult fusion of these roads has been completed to the extent it has, and that the operating situation has improved to the extent it has.
I have pointed out that we have in the Canadian National one of the significant sources of expenditure in the whole country. When you add to it the St. Lawrence seaway and agencies like the C.B.C. and others you
[Mr. Herridge.l
realize that government and instruments of government have come to play an enormous part in our national development. In my opinion the matter of capital expenditure which we shall be discussing this afternoon is so important that I propose to quote very briefly from the remarks of the president of the railway to show that, as I said, he has this matter in mind. I find the following at page 208 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the sessional committee on railways and shipping:

You told us there was a ruthless cutting of the capital budget to assist in this anti-inflationary drive; yet the money to be spent this year, as I understand it, is going to be more than last year. Does that mean that you started out with a great many more demands than last year and you cut down on that amount?	.	.
Mr Gordon: No. It means that the rate in spending had got to the point that we were involved in projects that could not be stopped. A great deal of our 1957 expenses arise out of commitments which have been entered into. For instance, there was the matter of equipment. We had placed orders for equipment last fall in connection with the diesel program. We had to do so in order to get delivery any time this year. I can give you a general picture in that respect; that we had estimated our requirements in the first approach, what we would need in the way of equipment requirements on the basis of traffic, our retirements of equipment and the figure for the utilization of equipment, and we budgeted for 7,600 units of equipment to take care of equipment of all kinds. But we cut that arbitrarily in half. We have not yet placed our orders for box cars because we are not satisfied with the prices quoted. We are now negotiating with the car companies telling them that we think their price is too high.
We have cut our planned dieselization program. We had it in mind this year to start complete dieselization by areas. You may remember that I said in previous committees that we would attack our dieselization program on the basis providing for specific services, in a five year program. We finished it last year and this year we started on complete dieselization on a territorial basis. Our plan was to start on each coast, west and east, and gradually complete it right towards central Canada. On the basis of that program we planned 654 units but we cut that down to 373 units. In other words, we reduced it by 281 units which meant about $58 million. That means that the progressive rate of our dieselization has been slowed down. We have just slowed the whole thing down on the basis that we are attempting to do too much and that the country is attempting to do too much having regard to its productive capacity.
I mention this and stress it, because not only the president of the national railway but other leading authorities have pointed out the desirability of this stretching out process, not merely because it will relieve the present pressure which is so great but because we may very well be glad two, three or four years from now to have, so to speak, some accumulated work at a time when the pressure is not so great; indeed, when the pressure might not be quite as great as we would like.

I wish to say a word about Trans-Canada Air Lines and its relation to the Canadian National. I think those are the only points I wish to raise. I simply repeat that we have here one of our great national enterprises, one of the great spenders of money, and I hope, notwithstanding that Mr. Gordon, as he indicated, has done certain cutting of expenditures, that if the pressures continue this year as they show some signs of doing he may be able to relieve the situation even more. I should like to say a few words on clause 1, inasmuch as I believe this is the last place where general remarks might be made. I have been greatly struck by the evidence before the committee dealing with the length of time involved from the filing of an application with the board of transport commissioners and the reaching of a decision in connection with fixing the rates the railway may charge.
Someone may say that this discussion is not in order at this time, but I say it is very much in order because, of course, upon what the board of transport commissioners may fix as rate charges depends to a great extent the amount of money for which the railway is obliged to ask in this annual vote. I am inclined to feel that the Minister of Transport might use some influence to see that the board of transport commissioners is not used just to provide a lawyers' field day. The president of the company has indicated that long before a decision is reached in some of these applications, his expenditures have already caught up with his income and in some cases have passed it. Either yesterday or today I read one paragraph in his report which indicated that.
It seems to me that if we are to expect the railways to be run on an efficient basis and to have an equal opportunity to succeed in the same way as we expect private corporations to do, then we must at all times be striving to put them in the same position. Mr. Chairman, I cannot see the steel companies or some organization like that, faced with rising costs, obliged to go through a long drawn out formula covering maybe eight months or nine months while some procedure was gone through in order to determine whether they were going to be allowed to meet those rising costs.
I strongly suggest that we remove any criticism of the board of transport commissioners over the lengthy time involved in these decisions. I realize that they are complicated but it seems to me that it is the old story of the lawyers' courtroom list. If we want to get on with the job, it can be done. If we want to stall around and see that it is handled one week from now or one month from now, then of course the list can be juggled; and that is what happens. I would therefore ask the Minister of Transport to do what he can to see that this time gap is shortened as much as possible.

From the point of view of the operator of a railway, having regard to the suggestions which have just been made by the hon. member for York West, I think it would seem to be an ideal situation, that is,

Canadian National Railways that all the railroads would have to do when they wished to increase their rates would be to go to the board of transport commissioners and ask for an increase. But surely the hon. gentleman realizes that increased rates, while adding to the revenues of the railroads, at the same time add substantially to the burden of those who must pay the increased rates of which he is speaking.
So far as I have been able to make out from examining the record of the recent increases in freight rates, there has not been at any time undue delay having regard, first of all, to the magnitude of the problem; second, its complexity; and third and perhaps foremost, the fact that it is not only the railroads' interests that are concerned but also the interests of a large body of people; and in the past that large body of people has desired to make representations to the board.
In the case last decided the board granted an interim increase of 7 per cent in July which was, I think, somewhat unusual. I do not say that in any critical sense at all. However, it seems to me that this action showed that on the part of the board there was an appreciation of the need of some immediate increase. Then after the matter had been fully and thoroughly debated before the board a further increase of 4 per cent was granted, effective on January 1 of this year.
As I believe hon. members know, the matter is still under review because, as we all appreciate, there are two factors that are constantly varying. Those two factors are, first, the volume of traffic; and second, the level of expenditures. Nothing stays sufficiently static so it can be dealt with in the same way as an ordinary piece of civil litigation before the courts. I do not think I would accept the implied criticism-perhaps that is a stronger word than I should use-or the suggestion that there has been delay on the part of the board. I fully appreciate the desire of the railways to get on as soon as possible, but I think we must steer a middle course between satisfying their demands instantly and giving those who are going to be affected by any increase the opportunity of being heard.

Certainly that was my understanding of what he said. I understood him to make a suggestion which in my opinion would be nothing but a slow motion sale of Trans-Canada Air Lines. It seems to me it is a good principle at this time to invoke the old motto, "Let well enough alone."
Without taking up the time of the committee unduly I want to say I know of no public institution that is serving the whole of Canada with greater satisfaction than Trans-Canada Air Lines. This is an institution that is not costing the taxpayers of Canada a cent, and which is operating efficiently in the interests of the whole country.
If we were pushed to it no doubt we could think of a hundred reasons why this great national asset should be retained for the use of the people of Canada, but if I had to select just one argument it would be this. If for any reason we made the great mistake of turning over to private enterprise this organization which has been so laboriously built up as a great successful public enterprise, we would of course have all the rules of private enterprise apply. One of the first effects of such a mistaken policy would be that the sections of the country which are now served by Trans-Canada Air Lines and which do not compare with the earning power of the whole system would very readily be abolished.
As I say, I do not intend to delay the committee, but I want to quote just one authority which I think will commend itself to the hon. member for York West. The authority to which I have referred said:
There is no necessity tonight to plunge into a discussion of the philosophical divergencies between socialism and Liberalism. It is not possible to draw a hard and fast line between individualism and collectivism. You cannot draw it either in theory or in practice. That is where the socialist makes a mistake. Let us not imitate that mistake. No man can be a collectivist alone or an individualist alone. He must be both an individualist and a collectivist. The nature of man is a dual nature. The character of the organisation of human 82715-203J
Canadian National Railways society is dual. Man is at once a unique being and a gregarious animal. For some purposes he must be collectivist, individualist . . . No view of society can possibly be complete which does not comprise within its scope both collective organisation and individual incentive. The whole tendency of civilisation is. however, towards the multiplication of the collective functions of society.

speechtext:
Before the minister answers those remarks, I would like to make it clear that the opposition to this measure by western members is due largely to the fact that if this is implemented we feel it will kill any opportunity there may be to have cash advances given.
The shortage of cash on the prairies in recent years, combined with the increasing cost of production, has had a very serious economic effect on a good many farmers. Some have had to leave their farms completely. I have known many farms which depend on grain and cattle raising where the herds have been completely ruined because there was not sufficient cash to pay debts and tax arrears in the fall of the year, with the result that the farmer was compelled to cut into his herd and sell some of his basic stock. The stock was not ready for sale, but he was compelled to sell it to get cash.
The fact is that the bill now proposed does nothing about relieving the grain grower in the west. Representations have been made on his behalf, and the minister must know what kind of representations have been made. He must know what has been the thinking Gf the people in the west. On December 3 last the farm union organization in their presentation to the federal-provincial conference had this to say:
The bank loan legislation implemented last year has not provided a solution. We feel that a permanent system of cash advances must be instituted to provide financial assistance to farmers during periods when due to congested storage facilities they cannot deliver their grain.
The minister knows they have not been able to deliver their grain. He knows what the situation is, and we need something which will meet that situation. These proposals will not do it. I thought perhaps we should try to block this legislation a little longer, but it is too late in the session to do that. We merely voice our opposition; and I endorse the words of the hon. member for Mackenzie when he says that if the government has anything else in mind we would like to know about it.

Mr. Speaker, I have not had the benefit of listening to all of this edifying debate, which revolves round a very small point.
References have been made to other plans for putting cash advances into the hands of the farmers. I have never received a well worked out plan; in fact I have never received any plan endorsed by any farm organization. We have heard vague talk from the opposition about cash advances, free of interest, on farm-stored grain. Various people have suggested ways in which the cash could be put out but no one, as far as I have been able to follow the debate, has suggested any way in which such an advance could be recovered.
Mr. Chairman, I did have a meeting with representative farm organizations a month or so ago, and at that time those present urged that this legislation be passed. They said they were not ready to put forward any other plan at this time but that they might be in the autumn. I said I would be glad to discuss such a plan with them. I mentioned the fact that the plan must be a scheme not only for putting out money but also for getting money back, because loans are loans, and when I am responsible for paying money out from the treasury I like to have some reasonable safeguard about getting that money repaid. Despite all the vague talk and nonsense spoken by the opposition, no definite alternative plan to the one now being considered has been put forward at any stage.
I say I have not followed the debate, but apparently the people in the west have followed it, because I have here a number of telegrams, which I think I should read. They have evidently been sent as the result of

people reading Hansard and noting that all opposition parties have opposed this legislation and voted against it. I just put these messages on record, because I have been told I do not know the real feeling of farmers about this legislation, and that farmers are all opposed to it.

I am reading the only wires I have. The first is dated March 29, and it is from Mr. Ben Plumer, chairman of the Alberta wheat pool, addressed to myself:
We are very much concerned with the delay in the passage of the interim financing act for grain. The improvements provided in this legislation can he of much greater importance to farmers this year than they would have been in any recent year. On behalf of Alberta wheat pool I would urge that the government make every possible effort to have this additional help provided, and it may be especially important this year.
The next wire is from Mr. G. L. Harrold, president of the Alberta federation of agriculture. It was addressed to myself, dated March 29:
Amendments to interim financing act considered most important to Alberta farmers. Urge government pass amendments this session to meet early fall needs. We reserve right to make further study and presentation toward still more acceptable plan.
Next, a telegram from Mr. A. W. Platt, president of the farmers' union of Alberta:
Alberta farmers' union believe farmers will need cash for farm-stored grain early next fall. We do not believe that the present act with the proposed amendments is the best scheme that can be devised but it will be very helpful. We therefore urge proposed amendments be passed at this session of the house. We believe these amendments worth while and will support them.
That is more than those who purport to speak for the farmers' union will do in this house, apparently. The next is from Mr. J. E. Brownlee, president of the United Grain Growers Limited, and this telegram is dated April 1, 1957.
The directors and officers of our company believe that a substantial demand for loans on farm-stored grain will develop again this fall and we are very anxious that the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act now before parliament be passed before the close of the present session so that assistance as provided therein may be made available to applicants by September first. We believe the terms of that act substantially meet views recently expressed to you and comprise the only provisions which can now be made effective before the next crop is harvested.
Should farm organizations agree on any other plan for future years your government will no doubt give same earnest consideration.
The next one is from George W. Robertson, secretary of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, and is dated March 29. It reads as follows:
In the opinion of our board there is urgent need for an adequate method of making available cash

advances against farm stored grain in the coming year. The interim finance act is the only avenue presently available for this purpose and since this legislation expires on June 1 we would strongly urge that the proposed amendments to this act be enacted at the present session of parliament so that terms of act with increased maximum advances may be available to producers. We shall look forward to a further discussion with you at a later date on the whole question of legislation for this purpose in an effort to reach agreement more in line with previous suggestions for a permanent solution of the problem.
The next wire is from W. J. Parker, president of the Manitoba wheat pool. It is dated April 1 and reads as follows:
I consider there is positive need for policy providing cash advances against farm stored grain. I urge that the proposed amendments to interim finance act be enacted forthwith so that its terms with increased maximum provisions may be available to producers not later than September 1 next. If western farm organizations can agree on better plan for this purpose at some later date we would welcome opportunity to present such to the federal government.

In their telegrams several of them have indicated that they wish to qualify because they all realize that they are going to find it extremely difficult to explain to the rank and file of their members why, in the year 1957, with our whole Canadian economy so buoyant, with the gross national product the highest in Canadian history, this sector of our Canadian economy should be in the position in which they cannot get the cash available at the moment so they can start the year's operations in a position where they have paid off their debts of a year ago and may be able to start paying cash for their petroleum products and other necessary expenses in connection with this spring's seeding operations.

I may say that this legislation was not spontaneous with the Department of Trade and Commerce; it was requested first by the western federation of agriculture at its meeting in Winnipeg. It was later endorsed by other farm meetings. There seemed to be general requests for this legislation. I read the relevant correspondence on an earlier occasion; I refer to the committee stage of this bill. As far as the remarks of the hon. member for Provencher are concerned, I will say that this government never fails to give serious consideration to any proposal put forward by the farm organizations, if it is a proposal of general application. We like to make sure that it is acceptable to all farm organizations.
I do not think the farmers of western Canada need to be told that the government is responsive to requests that are made through them. The wheat storage legislation resulted from suggestions made verbally to me in various farm meetings in the autumn of 1955 as a means of helping the farmer and that seemed to be the one method that all could agree on as being most helpful. Therefore, that legislation was put before parliament and passed. This legislation arises in the same way. My hon. friends may put themselves forward as being much wiser than are the leaders of the farm organizations but personally I do not accept that assertion.

I am sure that the minister's remarks of a few moments ago, when he read the telegrams, were quite enlightening to those perhaps who cannot see behind the telegrams. I am not concerned as to whether or not any feelers were put out that called

forth those telegrams, but the fact of the matter is that the minister, in a previous debate, made a statement to the effect that if the opposition continued to talk, perhaps this legislation would be left standing on the books. As my friend the hon. member for Wetaskiwin whispered to me a little while ago, what do the telegrams say? They say to the minister: "For goodness' sake, since we cannot get the loaf, please give us some crumbs". The minister read the telegrams. What do they say? Mr. Harrold's telegram indicated that they were willing to have this bill passed until some still more acceptable plans could be devised. The telegram from Mr. Platt said that it is not the best bill. The other telegrams indicated something along the same line. I do not think this group here can be accused of talking too much and wasting time. But the reason we have spoken and voted against it is not that we do not want the farmers to have some assistance but rather that we believe the farmers should get what they want; and they want something better. Within reason we believe that they should have something better. I hold in my hand a little handbook published by the Farmers' Union of Alberta as late as January, 1957. It is a condensed book on grain policy; it has 15 sections. Section 8 simply states as follows:
We favour a permanent system of cash advances on farm stored grain.
If that system were given to the farmers I do not think we would need any of this loan legislation or borrowing legislation or legislation giving authority to stand behind the banks when they lend farmers money on their grain of which they have not been able to dispose. That is the picture as I see it. Once again I want to say that we are not against the farmers being able to borrow money; of course we want them to be able to borrow money, but we are against giving them crumbs when we think they should be given the loaf.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM

I do not intend to go back into the matter of the arguments in favour of a system of cash advances on farm stored grain which occupied most of the time when this matter was being discussed at the resolution stage and again on second reading. However, I should like to point out again to the minister that the telegrams he has read, if they establish anything, establish the fact
Grain
that the farm organizations are expecting and hoping that some system of that sort will be put into effect rather than establishing the fact-as the minister seems to think the telegrams seem to indicate-that the farm organizations wanted this particular piece of legislation. All that they indicate is that they want it in lieu of something better. What they really want is something better and the something better they want is a system of cash advances. As far as clause 1 is concerned, subsection 2 of section 13A reads as follows:
No person who has received a guaranteed loan under this act before the 1st day of June, 1957 is, until such loan is repaid in full, entitled to receive a guaranteed loan referred to in subsection (1).
As the new legislation calls for or provides for a maximum loan of $3,000 whereas the old called for or provided for a maximum of only $1,500 I should like to ask the minister whether this provision is not likely to work a hardship on a considerable number of farmers who secured loans when the maximum was $1,500 and when that was all that they could secure. You will have many cases of men who have all kinds of wheat, or in other words all kinds of security. They received, we will say, the maximum amount or as much of a loan as they could get. When next fall comes along they will perhaps have not been able to pay back all of the $1,500 they obtained. They may be $100 short of paying it off or $200 or it might be only $50. But whatever the amount they may be short of paying it back, the fact is that they cannot get any further loan until it is paid back in spite of the fact that they would be eligible for a $3,000 loan under the new legislation whereas previously they were eligible for only a $1,500 loan. I should like to ask the minister whether there is any real necessity to have that particular subsection in the act and whether there should not be a provision so that the farmers, of whom there are likely to be a large number who will be in this situation, should be in the position in which they may get up to the maximum of $3,000 which is now provided for.
