speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 224, to incorporate the Windsor harbour commissioners.
He said: The purpose of this bill is to establish a corporation to manage and develop the harbour at Windsor, Ontario. The city council of Windsor, the senior and junior chambers of commerce have made representations in favour of the incorporation. The city has advised that upon enactment of the legislation it would vest in the proposed commissioners two lots of waterfront property having about 2,400 feet frontage and other smaller blocks of property. These civic bodies consider highly desirable, in the interests of proper and orderly development and expansion of the harbour, that control be vested in a local body. Increased activity expected to result from the completion of the St. Lawrence seaway is a further reason behind the proposal.
The bill is substantially similar to the Port Alberni Harbour Commissioners Act of 1947, and the Belleville Harbour Commissioners Act of 1952. At the present time the Department of Transport administers a public wharf in Windsor harbour approximately 850 feet in length from which an annual gross revenue of approximately $15,000 is derived. This wharf, together with the warehouse thereon, would

be placed under the administration and control of the harbour commissioners. The proposed commission will consist of three commissioners, one to be appointed by the city of Windsor and two by the governor in council. I am sure the house will not find the bill to be controversial and I hope it will be adopted readily.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION FOR MANAGEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF HARBOUR
speechtext:
On behalf of the official opposition, I am very glad to speak in support of this bill. I think the council and the citizens of the city of Windsor are to be complimented on taking this step. As we all know, there will be great developments in the whole St. Lawrence and great lakes area as a result of the St. Lawrence seaway. Sometimes I have been surprised that the cities so closely affected have not seemed to realize more clearly just what extensive developments there could be. Probably those cities which are in the forefront in realizing what the future may hold are the ones which will make the greatest progress.
Windsor is the first city, I think, to take the step of having a harbour commission set up, that is since this development has been commenced. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) will correct me if I am wrong, but I believe there are now seven similar harbour commissions, three of them in Ontario, at Belleville, Hamilton and Toronto, all of which were set up a good many years ago. There is one in Manitoba, the Winnipeg and St. Boniface harbour commission. There are three in British Columbia, New Westminster, North Fraser and Port Alberni. I know that all three harbour commissions in British Columbia have been very successful in their operations and have been largely responsible for the growth of industry in the respective areas under their jurisdiction.
I notice the present bill is in very much the same terms as the last bill of this nature which was passed, the Port Alberni Harbour Commissioners Act, which is chapter 42 of the statutes of 1947.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CORPORATION FOR MANAGEMENT AND DEVELOPMENT OF HARBOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first may I extend to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) the appreciation of the city of Windsor for his interest and his perseverance in bringing this bill before the house at the present time. May I also extend our appreciation to the Acting Leader of the Opposition for the very kind remarks he has made with respect to the city of Windsor and to the success of the Windsor harbour commission. This bill is the fruit of much study and investigation on the part of the Windsor junior chamber of commerce and the Windsor harbour promotion committee which was organized by the city council of the city of Windsor.
Situated as we are in Windsor on the Detroit river at the juncture of the upper great lakes with the lower lakes we have the city of Detroit on three sides of our community. Behind us is one of the most fertile agricultural areas in all Canada constituting the county of Essex and the county of Kent. In addition to this we have a very extensive manufacturing development there. We have one of the largest automobile manufacturing plants in the British Empire as well as a concentration of pharmaceutical industries.
The food processing plants in Essex and Kent counties supply the tables of the world with tomato products, pickles, relishes, corn, peas and a variety of other vegetables and fruits. The acres of garden under glass in Essex county are today supplying eastern Canada with fresh cucumbers and tomatoes.
6,	1957
Windsor Harbour Commissioners Soon our fertile gardens will supply the same markets with early tomatoes, early potatoes and other vegetables.
The counties of Essex and Kent were the original tobacco producers in Canada, this industry having come up from the United States through the state of Kentucky.
For many years we have supplied most of the table salt consumed in eastern Canada. Today we have a large and thriving salt mine a thousand feet below the surface of the land and of the Detroit river. This mine produces salt in rock form and it is shipped to many distant parts.
Much of our grain is processed into alcoholic beverages and allied alcoholic products which are shipped to the farthest corners of the globe and of course some of our grain is used as fodder for cattle.
I recall that a few years ago while in Bolivia, South America, though I am a teetotaller, I was glad to see in a shop window a product of Hiram Walker, Walkerville, Ontario. The International Playing Card Company also ships its products all over the world.
As I said a moment ago the city of Detroit is on three sides of our proposed port. This is the centre of a vast industrial and manufacturing area comprising the lower part of the state of Michigan, parts of Ohio and Indiana and the central United States. Within a radius of 50 miles of Windsor there is a population of four million people.
The city of Detroit has practically exhausted its port facilities and is not able to take full advantage of the many opportunities afforded that area by the development of the St. Lawrence seaway. For many years there has been an urgent need for adequate planning of our water resources so that they may be utilized more fully.
On the agricultural side, I would like to refer to some figures contained in a return made to an inquiry filed on January 22, 1956 giving the figures for the production of fall wheat, spring wheat, corn and soybeans for the years 1950 to 1956 inclusive. In 1955,
19,963,000	bushels of fall wheat were produced in the province of Ontario. Of this amount 2,056,000 bushels of fall wheat were produced in the county of Kent and 1,588,000 bushels were produced in the county of Essex in the same year. The total amount of fall wheat produced in the counties of Kent and Essex in that one year was 3,644,000 bushels. If one computes the percentage one will find that this represents about 18 per cent of all the fall wheat produced in the entire province of Ontario.
In 1955, 31,300,000 bushels of corn were produced in the province of Ontario and

Dealing now with manufacturing in this area we see that the total selling value of factory shipments from factories in the counties of Kent and Essex for the years 1952, 1953 and 1954-the only years for which figures are available-was as follows: In 1952 the county of Kent produced manufactured goods sold at a total value of $134,172,567, whereas the county of Essex produced $724,814,976. That is about three-quarters of a billion dollars. In 1953 Kent county produced $135,813,826 and the county of Essex produced $756,836,929. For the last year when figures are available, Kent county produced $121,273,639 and Essex county produced $550,513,764. But the fact remains that we have not developed our waterfront resources to their whole potential as they do not serve our factories and our farms to the fullest extent and do not attempt to serve an adequate portion of the Detroit river basin. Windsor is now in a position to meet the need existing in this area.
This port has presently abundant transportation facilities, that is to say, by rail, by truck and by air. The Canadian National Railways serves the area with connections by car ferry to the United States. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company also serves the port with connections over the New York Central line by tunnel to the United States. The New York Central line has its main line running from Chicago to New York with its Canadian terminal at Windsor, running from Windsor to Fort Erie. The Chesapeake and Ohio railway also serves the area with connections in Canada at Chatham, Sarnia, St. Thomas, Niagara Falls and other points and of course, with all points in the United States.


The Essex Terminal railway serves the port area linking with all main rail lines in Windsor running as far south as Amherstburg.
The international border of the United States is no problem since the transportation business is served by a tunnel for automobiles and trucks under the Detroit river. We also have a four-lane suspension bridge over the Detroit river. Then we have car ferries which shuttle across the river at several points. In addition the New York Central railroad has a double tube tunnel under the river for its purposes.
Now by air, Trans-Canada Air Lines serve Windsor and Detroit giving a freight and passenger service regularly from Toronto and points east-in fact, to all areas of the globe.
The trip to Toronto is made in less than an hour, a fact which it is interesting to note, while the distance by road is 250 miles. The Guest Air Lines give a direct service to this area from Mexico. Further air lines to distant countries are contemplated.
By road Windsor is the terminus of highway No. 2 to Quebec city and highway No. 3 to Niagara Falls. Recently a four-lane nonaccess highway, highway No. 401, has been serving this area. When the latter is completed it is expected that trucks and automobiles may drive through to Montreal without stopping-a distance of over 500 miles.
There are a number of areas available in the seven miles of waterfront in the city of Windsor which must be developed wisely and cautiously to attract commercial and industrial users. The Canadian National Railways is using approximately two miles of our undeveloped waterfront from the limits of the old town of Walkerville to the city limits. As a matter of fact, there are many miles of deep waterways available on the waterfront and in the small rivers leading into the Detroit river, as far south as Amherstburg. This is waiting development by large and small industrial users having to transport their products to distant ports of the world at the cheapest possible rate.
The Windsor harbour commission has as its purpose the providing of a pattern or framework for future development of the port by bulk storage, terminal warehouses or any other means found to be of advantage to the area. It must be anticipated that the needs will change from time to time and we must be prepared to meet the demand for years to come. To this end, appropriate and adequate facilities must be provided to handle both foreign and United States business as it is needed.
The present port-based industries in the Windsor area have an aggregate annual payroll of approximately $2 million, but the

Detroit area has port-based industries whose aggregate annual payroll is about $200 million. It can be seen, therefore, that the port of Windsor has a definite economic potential in the field of water transportation.
Toronto, Hamilton, Belleville and other ports in Canada have been similarly served by efficient harbour commissions which this bill seeks to provide for the city of Windsor and environment. Its purpose is to preserve deep water frontages, to control the development of the waterfront and to zone and rebuild the unused areas for the purpose of encouraging and servicing foreign trade as well as domestic, for the present and the future. As I see it, the benefits could be summarized as follows: First, it would mean lower freight rates to Canadian and overseas ports; second, it would mean the establishment of secondary industries, their bulk storage and their shippers; third, it would provide revenue to the port and to Canada from the United States business.
May I congratulate the minister once again for bringing forward this bill and may I say I feel it should be given the whole support of this house and I so recommend.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (for the Minister of Fisheries) moved

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF INTERIM CONVENTION ON CONSERVATION
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to implement the interim convention on conservation of north Pacific fur seals, signed at Washington on the 9th of February, 1957, by Canada, the United States of America, Japan, and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, and for carrying out Canada's obligations under the said interim convention.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. Watson MacNaughi (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF INTERIM CONVENTION ON CONSERVATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution relates to the interim convention signed at Washington on the 9th day of February, 1957 between Canada, the United States of America, Japan and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics for the regulation and control of fur seals in the North Pacific. The convention provides, among other things, for (a) the establishment of a North Pacific fur seal commission of four members, one from each of the signatories; (b) a six-year co-operative research program; (c) the prohibition of pelagic sealing except to a specified extent for research purposes; and (d) a sharing of the land kill so that Canada and Japan receive each year from the U.S.S.R. and the United States 15 per cent of the seal skins taken on the rookery islands by the two latter countries. The islands in question are; Pribilof islands owned by the United States, and the Commander and Robben islands under the control of the U.S.S.R.
It will be recalled that in 1911 a convention was signed by Great Britain for Canada, the United States, Japan and Russia in relation to fur seals in the North Pacific. The principal provisions of the newly signed convention which were absent in the 1911 convention are:
1.	The 1911 convention left research and management to the parties having control of the breeding areas. The other parties to the convention sharing the skins had no voice in the management of the fur seal herds. Under the new convention a commission is

to be established, composed of a representative of each government, which will have the duty of recommending to the four governments co-ordinated research programs and appropriate measures based on research, including the composition of the annual kill, the size of the herd to be maintained, the methods of sealing best suited to achieve the objectives of the convention. In general, all parties under the new convention are recognized as having an interest in the management of the seal herds of the north Pacific ocean.
2.	The new convention provides specifically for co-ordinated research to determine, among other things, the extent to which the food habits of fur seals affect commercial fish catches and the damage fur seals inflict on fishing gear. Having important commercial fisheries along some of the migration routes of the fur seals, this matter is of great importance to Canada. We will under the new convention have equal say in the matter of the over-all size of the seal herds and also be able to obtain the necessary scientific information as to the effect of predation by fur seals on stocks of fish of concern to us. It would have been difficult to obtain this information if all four governments had not joined in the co-operative research program.
3.	Each country undertakes an obligation to take a number of seals pelagically for research purposes; the rookery-owning countries also undertake the tagging of an appropriate number of seals.
The arrangement for the sharing of seal skins follows closely the provisions of the 1911 convention. We are to take 15 per cent from the United States of the commercial kill on the Pribilof islands and 15 per cent from the U.S.S.R. from the commercial kill on the Commander and Robben islands. Because the cost of research in the western Pacific will be heavier than on this side, a formula for compensating the U.S.S.R. during the years of heavy pelagic take for research is included in the convention. Under this formula, if in any year the number of seals taken for research around the Commander and Robben islands exceeds 2,000, we will forgo our share of seal skins for that year from the U.S.S.R., but in such case the United States will increase our share of the Pribilof take to the extent of 375 skins. This represents an estimated 50 per cent of what we would normally be getting from the U.S.S.R. in any one year.
Under the provisional fur sale agreement made between Canada and the United States in 1942, after Japan terminated the 1911 treaty, our share of skins from the Pribilof islands was increased from 15 per cent to

20 per cent. The Japanese share of the Pri-bilof islands' take was divided up between us and the United States. This was also our proportion of the skins under an agreement made between the United States and Great Britain on February 11, 1911, just before the quadripartite treaty of July, 1911. When the provisional fur seal agreement was made in 1942 and continued in 1947, it was understood that it was a temporary expedient until such time as a new agreement could be made to which the other interested countries would again be parties.
The newly signed convention exempts the Indians from the prohibition of pelagic sealing on the same conditions as contained in the previous conventions, that is that sealing would be allowed by Indians in canoes without firearms.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF INTERIM CONVENTION ON CONSERVATION
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this resolution. I think it is well that we should look at the background of the history of this industry. Seventy years ago this was a tremendously important industry on the west coast. The Victoria Sealing Company constructed special boats, which were built on the west coast, in order to carry out sealing operations. There were somewhere between 55 and 60 schooners operating out of Victoria, employing something in the nature of 1,500 men who were going out on the annual sealing expedition. They were carrying out their lawful profession of sealing on the high seas.
Just before the close of the last century United States fishermen, supported by armed vessels from the United States, endeavoured to close the Bering sea to our Canadian fishermen. There was a period of difficult situations occurring in which the Canadian fishermen were abused and every attempt was made to run our Canadian ships out of the Bering sea. It was only the persistence of the sealers from British Columbia, who in spite of the danger that they were running continued their lawful operations, that established the fact the Bering sea was not a closed sea to the United States. The result was that in 1891, 1892 and 1893 by agreement by United States and Great Britain, Canadian seamen refrained from fishing for seal in the Bering sea.
Then there followed a convention in Paris, France, under which an award was brought down in 1893 to the effect that the Victoria Sealing Company had every right to fish in the Bering sea; the rights of British Columbia seamen were established. Then, Great Britain, in order to find the means of co-operating with the United States and not being anxious to pursue the matter further, agreed that compensation should be paid, first of all to
North Pacific Fur Seals the Victoria Sealing Company and then subsequently to any company which might be operating there. These claims were never paid and Victoria lost a great deal of business from the prohibition against their sealers. A lot of these special shipbuilding operations, which were carried out in the shipyards there were lost also.
However, it was as a result of the efforts made by the British Columbia fishermen that Canada established her right to a portion of the pelts which were eventually taken in the Pribilof and Commander islands. Under the treaty of 1911, Canada received 15 per cent of the pelts which were killed in the Pribilof islands on the American side and of those killed on the Russian and Japanese side of the Pacific. I think I am correct in saying that never at any time did Canada receive her share of the 15 per cent of the Russian seals.
These fur seals spend the period from November to June each year off the west coast of British Columbia, and particularly off the west coast of Vancouver island. There are in the herd something over 2 million fur seals. It has been estimated that these consume about 15 pounds of fish per day per seal. You can see, therefore, what great havoc is wrought on our stocks of salmon and other fish. In fact, I wonder whether, if there were no fur seals or if the number were reduced, it would be necessary for the Department of Fisheries this year to impose regulations prohibiting trolling on the west coast during the winter months for spring salmon. It seems to me that British Columbia suffers very considerably from the ravages of the fur seal herd. British Columbia gets nothing in return.
I am going to make a suggestion that the moneys which are derived from the sale of Canada's share of the pelts should be used directly for the benefit of British Columbia fishermen. Instead of having these moneys placed in the consolidated revenue fund, they should be used entirely for the development of the fisheries on the Pacific coast because British Columbian salmon are feeding this herd all during the winter months. There is a precedent for that sort of thing being done. As the parliamentary assistant will know, under the Halifax fisheries commission of 1877 there was a sum of $5,500,000 paid in compensation which was to go to the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland. Newfoundland received $1 million, leaving the sum of $4,500,000 out of which, by act of 1882, it was agreed to pay the interest on the actual bounties to those who were engaged in the Atlantic fisheries. This amount was fixed at $160,000, to be distributed so much per ton per vessel; so

North Pacific Fur Seals much per man per boat and so much to each boat owner. It seems to me that what is fair for the Atlantic coast fishermen is also fair for the Pacific coast fishermen.
That is the reason I feel entitled to suggest that the moneys derived from the sale of the pelts of the fur seals should be devoted exclusively to the development of the Pacific coast fisheries. I hope the parliamentary assistant will discuss this suggestion with his colleagues. Because he comes from the Atlantic coast he will realize how beneficial it is to the fishermen on the east coast. They receive this advantage and I am certain he would not wish to deny a similar advantage to the fishermen on the west coast.
I am pleased that under this convention will be set up the commission which will make inquiries into the development and feeding habits of these fur seals. With the reduction of the quantity of the salmon run it is extremely doubtful at the present time whether we can afford to allow this herd of fur seals to develop. Surely food, as originating from our salmon, is more valuable to the world than the fur pelts which are obtained from the kill of the seal.
Six years has been set as a period during which a research program will be conducted, I suggest to ascertain whether it is really worth while perserving these seals. I would like to call the parliamentary assistant's attention to the fact that in recent years cubs of these fur seals have been discovered in increasing numbers off the west coast of Vancouver island. Originally all the cubs were given birth on the Pribilof islands and young cubs were not found off Vancouver island. This would indicate to me that the large herd of fur seals are finding it difficult to get sufficient food in the northern waters and that they are now moving south because the cubs are being born elsewhere than in the northern islands.
I had occasion to write to the minister calling his attention to the incidence of some of these cubs being found a couple of years ago. Perhaps I might refresh the parliamentary assistant's memory on that point and ask him to make quite certain that this is one of the matters the commission will take into consideration during their research.
I was going to ask a question regarding the Indians. I take it that the Indians can kill as many seals as they see fit or as many as they require for their own purposes providing they are killed from canoes with spears. I understand there are no restrictions on the number of seals which Indians can kill with spears from canoes but of course they are not allowed to use firearms.

I believe I am correct in saying that the number of seals to be killed at sea is as follows: Japan, 3,250; United States, 1,750; Russia, 1,250 and Canada 750. If those figures are correct they do not quite agree with the 2,000 limit which the parliamentary assistant mentioned and I would like to be informed on that matter.
With those reservations and with the earnest hope that arrangements will be made so that the moneys derived from the pelts of these animals will be used for the benefit of Pacific coast fishermen, we are in agreement with the adoption of this convention.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF INTERIM CONVENTION ON CONSERVATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the background and history of the fur seal situation has been pretty well covered in general outline by the parliamentary assistant and by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich so I shall not attempt to cover that ground at this time, but there are one or two matters with which I would like to deal.
I would like to say at the outset that I am very pleased to have the statement from the parliamentary assistant that this new treaty is going to bring in to the fur seal situation the same principles of management that have been incorporated in treaties in respect to the sockeye salmon and other fisheries treaties to which Canada has been a party in recent years. I think that represents a definite step forward in relation to this question.
I am also glad to note that definite provision is being made for an analysis through scientific study of the effect of the fur seal upon our great Pacific fisheries on the west coast. I certainly agree with the emphasis placed on this consideration by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. The hon. member brought forward a most interesting suggestion in relation to the possible direct return to the fishermen on the Pacific coast of the benefits which Canada receives from the fur seal kill, because of the effect the fur seal has upon the plenitude of our commercial fisheries, based on the fact that embodied in the setting up of the commission provision is made for a real study of this relationship. It is fitting that the benefit of that study should accrue to those who are concerned with the commercial fisheries in British Columbia.
There is one additional matter to which I think consideration should be given in this connection because if anyone has a first claim upon these benefits I feel it should be the aboriginal population of the coastal areas of British Columbia. In his opening remarks the parliamentary assistant mentioned that the new treaty as proposed carries forward in the same terms the rights of

the native Indians of the west coast to utilize these fur seals for food. I have recently received some representation on this point from some of the Indians who dwell in my constituency. They have their eyes on the fact that Canada is entering this treaty and have a genuine interest in this particular matter. I think perhaps we should view this situation in its true perspective.
I have before me some rather interesting statistics on the fur seal kill which came to my hands in a copy of the report of the ninth British Columbia natural resources conference before which a paper was delivered by two gentlemen from the fisheries research board of Canada biological station at Nanaimo, British Columbia, namely, Messrs. M. P. Shepard and J. C. Stevenson. On page 183 of this report they set out in table form the history of the fur seal kill in the period beginning 1876 to 1955 and in this table it shows that during the period from 1876 to 1910 inclusive all of the kill of fur seals was pelagic, done by Canadian sealing vessels, and I assume that, absorbed in these figures, were the kills made by the aborigines during that period of time. But following 1910 the pelagic killing of the seals and the operation of sealing vessels ceased.
The figures are set forth for the aboriginal kill during those years and it shows in the period 1911 to 1915 the average kill was 815, from 1916 to 1920 the average kill as 319, from 1921 to 1925 it was 2,880, from 1926 to 1930 it was 2,406, from 1931 to 1935, it was 1,266, and from 1936 to 1940 it was 1,300. Then in the period from 1941 to 1945 the kill dropped to 15 and then a note indicates that this reflected the interference due to wartime conditions. In the period 1946 to 1950 the kill was 124, then in 1951 it was 534, in 1952 it was 28 and in 1953 it was 54. Then during 1954 and 1955 no kills are recorded and a footnote explains that surveys by the Department of Fisheries in 1954 and 1955 revealed that the Canadian coastal Indians possessed no serviceable aboriginal equipment, that is to say canoes and spears suitable for taking fur seals.
Now I think it is important that the house should realize the situation, for while the parliamentary assistant tells us that the historical rights of the Indians are protected benefits are not much more than theoretical.
As I mentioned earlier, I have received some recent representations on the subject pointing out to me that the non-availability of deer has meant a decrease in the food supply in recent years along the west coast of Vancouver island. Undoubtedly as far as the Indians along the west coast of Vancouver island are concerned, they would like
North Pacific Fur Seals to be allowed the privilege of taking a reasonable number of these seals for food and for their own use as they require them, with something a little more modern than canoes and spears. I think that this is a problem that should be considered because there are not a great many Indians along the west coast and in parts of the country where they do, from time to time, have a legitimate need for access to food supplies. Furthermore they should have this access in a manner which would be a little easier than going out over the Pacific breakers in canoes with spears, as their ancestors did.
This matter should be taken into consideration in the light of the suggestion made by the member for Esquimalt-Saanich. If in the over-all consideration of national policy and our arrangements with other nations having rights and interests in the fur seal kill it is necessary for us to agree to a limitation of this kind upon the taking for their own use of the seals by the Indians we might well consider some alternative form of benefit which might be given to them in recognition of the fact that they have not available to them facilities which for some good reason they feel should be their right.
I am not going to expand upon this matter any further at the present time but I do feel that, along with some of the other considerations that are involved in this treaty and which were introduced into discussion by the parliamentary assistant and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, this is something that we should have in our minds when we consider the adoption of the bill which will ratify this treaty.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

subtopic: AMENDMENT SUBSTITUTING JUDGE FOR STIPENDIARY MAGISTRATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Territorial Lands Act was passed in 1950. This act replaced the old Dominion Lands Act and is now the statute which governs the administration, control and disposition of the lands in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, with the exception of quartz and placer mining rights in the Yukon Territory.
In the Territorial Lands Act a simple procedure was provided for taking proceedings before a stipendiary magistrate to evict persons who were trespassing upon or unlawfully occupying crown lands. The power to hear such proceedings was given to a stipendiary magistrate and could not be exercised by anyone else. When the Yukon Act and the Northwest Territories Act were revised and came into effect on the 1st April, 1955, the appointment of stipendiary magistrates was no longer necessary and the positions were abolished. The amendment proposed by the bill will allow the proceedings to be heard before a judge of the territorial court.
There is nobody now to judge these cases of eviction. The amendment proposed by the bill is very simple: it will allow the proceedings to be heard before a judge of the territorial court.

Territorial Lands Act

maintopic: CURRENCY. MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AMENDMENT TO INCREASE REMEDY ALLOWANCE FOR TEN-CENT PIECES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the face of it this is a very simple measure, and I think it is essentially a very simple measure. I took a little trouble to inform myself about some of the background of the mint and its activities and I should like to put on the record two or three facts which interested me and which


I think are not wholly irrelevant. I will reassure members of the house by saying that I shall not take more than three or four minutes with the information that I wish to put on the record.
First of all, I should like to recall that apparently we find the first known coins about 700 B.C., and the first British coin is tentatively placed in the second century B.C. We come then to the history of the royal mint in London which began in Anglo-Saxon times, but the thing that interested me was that coinage was not then confined to one place nor did the sovereign insist too strongly on the right of coining which, according to the civil law maxim, "is inherent in the bones of princes."

maintopic: CURRENCY. MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AMENDMENT TO INCREASE REMEDY ALLOWANCE FOR TEN-CENT PIECES
speechtext: Pardon?

maintopic: CURRENCY. MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AMENDMENT TO INCREASE REMEDY ALLOWANCE FOR TEN-CENT PIECES
speechtext:
"Inherent in the bones of princes". Nevertheless, the ecclesiastics did a bit of coining in those days too. I am referring to an article on the royal mint and its branches found in the Canadian Georgrahic Journal, volume 3, 1931, at page 57. In part it has this to say:
. . . nor did the sovereign insist too strongly on the right of coining which, according to the Civil Law maxim, is "inherent in the bones of princes", for we find the Archbishop of Canterbury and other ecclesiastical dignitaries issuing their own coins alongside those of the King. Indeed, for many years after coinage became fully recognized as a prerogative of the crown we find the management of the mints, as of other departments of government, largely controlled by ecclesiastics, perhaps because they alone, as a class, had the necessary education.
There is one further passage I should like to put on the record.
As late as 1548, according to Ruding, Bishop Latimer, in a sermon at St. Paul's inveighed against bishops and other churchmen occupying stations in the mint. "They are," he said of them, "otherwise occupied .	. . some comptrollers of
myntes. Well, well, ... I would fayne knowe who comptrolleth the devill at home at his parishe, while he comptrolleth the mynte?" . . . The saying is that since priests have been mynters money hath been worse than it was before."

maintopic: CURRENCY. MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AMENDMENT TO INCREASE REMEDY ALLOWANCE FOR TEN-CENT PIECES
speechtext: They must be minters now because it is a lot worse.

maintopic: CURRENCY. MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AMENDMENT TO INCREASE REMEDY ALLOWANCE FOR TEN-CENT PIECES
speechtext:
I continue:
"And they say that the evilnesse of money hath made all things dearer." It may he fitting at this point to offer the assurance that the present high cost of living is not due to church interference in matters of coinage.
I apologize for this interlude, and I now come to the bill, which is very simple. The explanatory note indicates that its purpose is to increase the allowance for error in the manufacture of the 10 cent piece. The note is in these words:
The purpose of this bill is to increase the remedy allowance for 10 cent pieces. The new high speed rolling mills, which were installed in the mint

early in 1956, cannot give as precise a thickness as former mills. The proposed new remedy allowance is the same as that in the United States.
It is a substantial increase in the remedial allowance. But if my arithmetic is good, it is still only about one quarter of one per cent. Inquiry from the mint shows that so far as loss is concerned, there is no reason to expect loss because the error is just as likely to be one way as the other. I therefore think the machine can be regarded neither as moral nor immoral but as being quite amoral and that we have no reason to think it is discriminating either for or against.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CURRENCY. MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AMENDMENT TO INCREASE REMEDY ALLOWANCE FOR TEN-CENT PIECES
speechtext: Or are they just tender?

maintopic: CURRENCY. MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AMENDMENT TO INCREASE REMEDY ALLOWANCE FOR TEN-CENT PIECES
speechtext: I am quite serious in that question. My understanding is that these coins are legal tender up to a point; and I do not believe that their being legal tender depends on anyone coming along and weighing them. I would think it depends on the imprimatur of the government of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: CURRENCY. MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AMENDMENT TO INCREASE REMEDY ALLOWANCE FOR TEN-CENT PIECES
speechtext: I think the point is that there is a committee, as I have said, which from time to time inquires about the efficiency of the mint. This bill will indicate that this committee will disregard a tolerance of the nature referred to in the bill.

maintopic: CURRENCY. MINT AND EXCHANGE FUND ACT AMENDMENT TO INCREASE REMEDY ALLOWANCE FOR TEN-CENT PIECES
speechtext: May I ask the parliamentary assistant this question since he has told us- and the bill also tells us-that this machine is in operation in the United States and that the same degree of inaccuracy is found there. Might that be one reason why on the United States coins we find the words "In God we Trust"?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have consulted with hon. gentlemen opposite and I understand that there would be no objection to proceeding now with the amendment to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. The minister is here. It is No. 1 on today's order paper.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED AWARDS AND LEVY
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider Bill No. 157, to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.
On clause 1-Number of acres for which award may be made.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED AWARDS AND LEVY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the members in the committee are in very good humour this afternoon and I do not propose to make any extended remarks. This bill was referred to the committee on agriculture and colonization. The minister was good enough to have his officials on hand to answer questions. While legislation never measures up to the expectations of opposition members who would like something better, nevertheless this legislation makes provision for payments which the minister anticipates will be a good deal higher that would have been possible under the previous legislation. It also makes provision for these payments to be
made without any additional levy on the people concerned. It was the hope of all hon. members who were at the committee meetings that at some stage it might be possible to get a more comprehensive plan that would provide assistance for farmers in all parts of Canada. But those who are from the prairie area are glad that this amendment has been brought forward this year.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 2-Blocks ineligible for award.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED AWARDS AND LEVY
speechtext: It is very hard to decide whether or not this is a good section. I think that under subsection (a) the farmer will be worse off under this amendment than he would have been before, but under subsection (b), he will be better off. On balance, he will probably gain more as a result of (b) than he will lose as a result of (a), and therefore we must support the section.
